title: Animal Kingdom
description: Grade 11 Biology: basis of animal classification (symmetry, coelom, segmentation, notochord), the major invertebrate phyla, and phylum Chordata with its vertebrate classes.

topics.title: Basis of Animal Classification
topics.concept:
The animal kingdom is vast, so animals are classified using a set of fundamental features common across phyla, rather than their outward form. The key criteria are:

  • Levels of organisation — cellular (cells loosely arranged, e.g. sponges), tissue (cells form tissues, e.g. cnidarians), organ, and organ-system level (e.g. higher animals).
  • Symmetry — asymmetrical (no plane divides it into equal halves, e.g. sponges), radial (any plane through the centre gives equal halves, e.g. cnidarians, echinoderms) or bilateral (only one plane gives two equal halves, e.g. most higher animals).
  • Germ layers — diploblastic (two layers: ectoderm and endoderm, e.g. cnidarians) or triploblastic (three layers, with a middle mesoderm, e.g. flatworms onwards).
  • Coelom (body cavity) — acoelomate (no cavity, e.g. flatworms), pseudocoelomate (a false cavity, e.g. roundworms) or coelomate (a true body cavity lined by mesoderm, e.g. annelids onwards).
  • Segmentation — whether the body is divided into repeating segments (metamerism), e.g. earthworm.
  • Notochord — a flexible rod along the back. Animals with a notochord (at some stage) are chordates; those without are non-chordates (invertebrates).

These shared features let biologists group millions of animals into about a dozen major phyla and trace their evolutionary relationships.

examples.problem: Example 1: Distinguish radial and bilateral symmetry, with an example of each.
examples.solution:
Symmetry is judged by planes of equal halves.

  • Radial: any plane through the central axis gives equal halves (e.g. a starfish, jellyfish).
  • Bilateral: only one plane gives two equal (mirror) halves (e.g. a human, insect).
examples.answer: Radial symmetry (any central plane gives equal halves, e.g. starfish) vs bilateral symmetry (only one plane does, e.g. human).

examples.solution:
Count the germ layers.

  • Diploblastic: two germ layers (ectoderm and endoderm), e.g. cnidarians.
  • Triploblastic: three layers (with a middle mesoderm), e.g. flatworms and higher animals.
examples.answer: Diploblastic animals have two germ layers (e.g. cnidarians); triploblastic animals have three, including a mesoderm (e.g. flatworms onwards).

examples.problem: Example 3: What is a coelom, and how does an acoelomate differ from a coelomate?
examples.solution:
The coelom is a body cavity.

  • A coelom is a true body cavity lined by mesoderm.
  • Acoelomates have no body cavity (e.g. flatworms); coelomates have a true coelom (e.g. annelids onwards).
examples.answer: A coelom is a true mesoderm-lined body cavity; acoelomates lack it (flatworms), coelomates have it (annelids onwards).

recap:
• Animals are classified by fundamental features: levels of organisation, symmetry, germ layers, coelom, segmentation and the notochord.
  • Symmetry: asymmetrical / radial / bilateral; germ layers: diploblastic / triploblastic.
  • Coelom: acoelomate / pseudocoelomate / coelomate.
  • Presence of a notochord separates chordates from non-chordates.

quiz.q: An animal that can be divided into two equal halves by only one plane shows ___ symmetry.
quiz.explanation: Bilateral symmetry means only one plane gives two equal (mirror) halves.

quiz.q: A true body cavity lined by mesoderm is called a:
quiz.explanation: The coelom is a true, mesoderm-lined body cavity.

topics.title: The Major Invertebrate (Non-Chordate) Phyla
topics.concept:
The non-chordates (invertebrates) lack a notochord. The major phyla, roughly in increasing complexity, are:

  • Porifera (sponges) — cellular level; have pores (ostia) and canals; water-canal system; mostly marine. E.g. Sycon, Spongilla.
  • Cnidaria (Coelenterata) — tissue level; radial symmetry, diploblastic; have stinging cells (cnidoblasts). E.g. Hydra, jellyfish, corals, sea anemone.
  • Ctenophora — 'comb jellies'; marine, radially symmetrical, diploblastic; show bioluminescence.
  • Platyhelminthes (flatworms) — bilateral, triploblastic, acoelomate; dorsoventrally flattened; many are parasites. E.g. Planaria, liver fluke, tapeworm.
  • Aschelminthes (roundworms) — bilateral, triploblastic, pseudocoelomate; many are parasites. E.g. Ascaris, Wuchereria (causes filariasis).
  • Annelida — the first segmented, true coelomate animals; bilateral, triploblastic. E.g. earthworm, Nereis, leech.
  • Arthropoda — the largest phylum; jointed appendages, chitinous exoskeleton, open circulation. E.g. insects, prawn, spider, scorpion, Apis (honey bee).
  • Mollusca — the second largest phylum; soft body usually with a calcareous shell. E.g. snail, octopus, Pila, mussel.
  • Echinodermata — marine; spiny skin, water-vascular system, radial symmetry in adults. E.g. starfish, sea urchin.
  • Hemichordata — a small group once placed with chordates; e.g. Balanoglossus.

examples.problem: Example 1: Name the largest animal phylum and give two of its features.
examples.solution:
The largest phylum is Arthropoda.

  • Features: jointed appendages and a chitinous exoskeleton.
  • (Also open circulatory system.) Examples include insects and prawns.
examples.answer: Arthropoda; features include jointed appendages and a chitinous exoskeleton (e.g. insects, prawns).

examples.problem: Example 2: Which phylum is the first to show true segmentation and a true coelom?
examples.solution:
Segmentation and a true coelom first appear together in one phylum.

  • Annelida (e.g. earthworm) is the first segmented, true coelomate phylum.

examples.problem: Example 3: Name the special cells of Cnidaria and one example animal.
examples.solution:
Cnidarians have stinging cells.

  • Special cells: cnidoblasts (stinging cells used for defence/capture of prey).
  • Example: Hydra (also jellyfish, corals).
examples.answer: Cnidarians have stinging cells called cnidoblasts; an example is Hydra.

recap:
• Porifera (sponges, pores), Cnidaria (cnidoblasts, radial), Ctenophora (comb jellies).
  • Platyhelminthes (flatworms, acoelomate), Aschelminthes (roundworms, pseudocoelomate).
  • Annelida = first segmented true coelomates; Arthropoda = largest phylum (jointed legs, chitin exoskeleton).
  • Mollusca (soft body, shell), Echinodermata (spiny skin, water-vascular system), Hemichordata.

quiz.q: The largest phylum in the animal kingdom is:
quiz.explanation: Arthropoda, with jointed appendages and a chitin exoskeleton, is the largest phylum.

quiz.q: True segmentation (metamerism) and a true coelom are first seen together in:
quiz.explanation: Annelids (e.g. earthworm) are the first segmented, true coelomate animals.

topics.title: Phylum Chordata and the Vertebrate Classes
topics.concept:
Members of phylum Chordata have, at some stage of life, three defining features: a notochord, a dorsal hollow nerve cord, and paired pharyngeal gill slits. They are bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic, coelomate animals. Chordata is divided into three subphyla: Urochordata (e.g. Ascidia), Cephalochordata (e.g. Branchiostoma/Amphioxus) and the largest, Vertebrata.

In Vertebrata, the notochord is replaced (during development) by a vertebral column (backbone), and they have a well-developed brain protected by a cranium. Vertebrates are grouped into five classes:

  • Pisces (fishes) — aquatic; breathe with gills; have fins and scales; cold-blooded; mostly egg-laying. E.g. Labeo (rohu), shark, Catla.
  • Amphibia — live both in water and on land; breathe through gills, lungs and moist skin; cold-blooded; lay eggs in water. E.g. frog, toad, salamander.
  • Reptilia — creeping land animals with dry, scaly skin; breathe by lungs; cold-blooded; lay shelled eggs on land. E.g. lizard, snake, turtle, crocodile.
  • Aves (birds) — body covered with feathers; forelimbs modified into wings; have a beak; warm-blooded; lay eggs. E.g. crow, pigeon, any bird.
  • Mammalia — have hair/fur and mammary glands (feed young on milk); warm-blooded; most give birth to young ones (viviparous). E.g. human, cow, whale, bat.

Birds and mammals are warm-blooded (homeothermic) — they keep a constant body temperature; the other three classes are cold-blooded (poikilothermic).

examples.problem: Example 1: State the three fundamental features that define a chordate.
examples.solution:
All chordates share these (at some life stage).

  • A notochord.
  • A dorsal hollow nerve cord.
  • Paired pharyngeal gill slits.
examples.answer: A notochord, a dorsal hollow nerve cord, and paired pharyngeal gill slits.

examples.problem: Example 2: Which two vertebrate classes are warm-blooded, and what does that mean?
examples.solution:
Warm-blooded animals control their temperature.

  • Aves (birds) and Mammalia are warm-blooded (homeothermic).
  • They keep a constant body temperature regardless of the surroundings.
examples.answer: Birds (Aves) and mammals are warm-blooded — they maintain a constant body temperature.

examples.problem: Example 3: Give two features that distinguish mammals from other vertebrates.
examples.solution:
Mammals have unique features.

  • Presence of hair/fur on the body.
  • Presence of mammary glands to feed the young on milk.
examples.answer: Mammals have hair/fur on the body and mammary glands that feed their young on milk.

recap:
• Chordata: notochord + dorsal hollow nerve cord + pharyngeal gill slits (at some stage); subphyla Urochordata, Cephalochordata, Vertebrata.
  • In vertebrates the notochord is replaced by a vertebral column; five classes: Pisces, Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves, Mammalia.
  • Aves and Mammalia are warm-blooded; fishes, amphibians and reptiles are cold-blooded.
  • Mammals have hair and mammary glands and are mostly viviparous.

quiz.q: Which feature is NOT one of the three defining chordate characters?
quiz.explanation: Jointed legs are an arthropod feature; the three chordate features are notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord and gill slits.

quiz.q: Mammary glands and hair on the body are characteristic of:
quiz.explanation: Hair and mammary glands are defining features of mammals.

questions.q: Sponges show which level of body organisation?
questions.explanation: Sponges (Porifera) have the cellular level of organisation.

questions.q: An animal divisible into equal halves by any plane through the central axis has ___ symmetry.
questions.explanation: Radial symmetry allows any central plane to make equal halves.

questions.q: Animals with three germ layers are called:
questions.explanation: Triploblastic animals have three germ layers, including a mesoderm.

questions.q: A true body cavity lined by mesoderm is a:
questions.explanation: The coelom is a true mesoderm-lined body cavity.

questions.q: Stinging cells (cnidoblasts) are found in phylum:
questions.explanation: Cnidarians have stinging cnidoblasts, e.g. Hydra.

questions.q: Flatworms (Platyhelminthes) are:
questions.explanation: Flatworms are acoelomate (no body cavity).

questions.q: Ascaris (roundworm) belongs to which phylum?
questions.explanation: Roundworms like Ascaris are Aschelminthes (pseudocoelomate).

questions.q: The first segmented, truly coelomate animals belong to:
questions.explanation: Annelids (earthworm) are the first segmented true coelomates.

questions.q: The largest phylum, with jointed appendages and a chitin exoskeleton, is:
questions.explanation: Arthropoda is the largest phylum.

questions.q: Starfish and sea urchins, with spiny skin and a water-vascular system, are:
questions.explanation: Echinodermata have spiny skin and a water-vascular system.

questions.q: Which is one of the three defining features of chordates?
questions.explanation: A notochord is one of the three chordate features.

questions.q: In vertebrates, the notochord is replaced by a:
questions.explanation: Vertebrates have a vertebral column in place of the notochord.

questions.q: Animals that breathe through gills, have fins and scales, and are cold-blooded belong to class:
questions.explanation: Fishes (Pisces) have gills, fins and scales and are cold-blooded.

questions.q: Birds (Aves) are characterised by feathers and:
questions.explanation: Birds have feathers and forelimbs modified into wings; they are warm-blooded.

questions.q: Which two classes of vertebrates are warm-blooded?
questions.explanation: Only birds (Aves) and mammals are warm-blooded.

questions.q: Adult starfish show radial symmetry, but their larvae are bilaterally symmetrical. This suggests echinoderms evolved from:
questions.explanation: The bilateral larva indicates a bilaterally symmetrical ancestry, with radial symmetry secondarily acquired.

questions.q: A true coelom is an advantage because it:
options: Allows organs to develop, move and be cushioned independently of the body wall
Removes the need for a gut
questions.explanation: A fluid-filled coelom gives space for organ development and movement, cushioning the organs.

questions.q: A worm is bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic and has a fluid 'false' cavity not fully lined by mesoderm. It is a:
questions.explanation: A body cavity not fully lined by mesoderm is a pseudocoelom, characteristic of Aschelminthes.

questions.q: Why are amphibians tied to water for reproduction even though they live on land?
options: They lay eggs without shells that must stay moist, and gametes need water
questions.explanation: Amphibian eggs lack a protective shell and are laid in water; reproduction depends on a watery environment.

questions.q: Reptiles colonised dry land more successfully than amphibians largely because they have:
options: Dry scaly skin and shelled eggs that resist water loss
questions.explanation: Dry scales reduce water loss and shelled (amniotic) eggs can develop on land, freeing reptiles from water.

questions.q: A bat flies and a whale swims, yet both are classed as mammals because they:
options: Have hair and feed their young on milk from mammary glands
questions.explanation: Despite different lifestyles, hair and milk-producing mammary glands make both mammals.
